article.overview: A soil mechanical properties tester is a class of instrument that measures the strength-related behaviour of lunar regolith, such as cohesion, internal friction angle, density and bearing capacity. Measurements are made by pressing a plate or cone into the soil, digging or trenching it, or turning a shear vane in it, and then interpreting the force and displacement data with soil mechanics theory. The data are needed to design lander footpads, anchors, excavation equipment and any future surface construction. The catalogue entry describes a generic payload class rather than one standard flight instrument, so the examples in this article are individual historical and proposed instruments, not a universal specification.
article.description: Lunar regolith is a loose, fine-grained layer of broken rock and glass that covers the Moon's surface. Its mechanical behaviour differs from that of most terrestrial soils, which are usually moist, cemented or differently graded. A soil mechanical properties tester gathers direct or indirect evidence of how the regolith resists loading, digging and penetration. Historically, this evidence came from the Surveyor surface sampler, which dug, scraped and trenched the surface while its motor current was recorded, and from the Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer, which pushed a plate or cone into the ground while recording force against depth. Apollo-era analyses also used trenching and vane shear observations [2]. A modern instrument would need to measure the properties most relevant to its mission, such as strength at the surface, strength with depth, or both.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of such an instrument is partly scientific and partly engineering. Scientifically, the strength parameters help to characterise the regolith's physical state, including its density and porosity, and how these change with depth and across the surface [7][2]. Engineering uses include supplying data for footpads, anchors, excavation tools and surface structures, and checking whether soil can support a lander or rover before hardware is committed [3]. Both Surveyor and Apollo measurements were used in this way, although the sources consulted do not show the full extent of their use in later design decisions [1][4].
article.operating_principle: An instrument of this class applies a controlled load to the regolith and records the response. In a penetrometer, a plate or cone is pushed into the soil and the force is recorded as a function of depth. The Apollo SRP recorded penetration on a drum through a cable and a calibrated spring, with a reference plane resting on the surface [4]. Interpreting penetration resistance requires a failure model in which cohesion and friction angle control the bearing capacity of the cone or plate, and several combinations of those two parameters can fit the same data [4]. A surface sampler performs bearing tests (pressing its scoop or plate into the surface), trenching tests and impact tests. For Surveyor 7, motor current was recorded during the bearing and trenching tests and, with preflight calibrations, converted into forces [1]. A shear vane tests strength by rotating a bladed element in the soil. In one laboratory study, a modified shear vane was judged the most promising of the instruments tested [3].
article.scientific_importance: Lunar regolith is not well described by terrestrial soil models. Apollo-era and Surveyor-era investigations showed that the regolith has interlocking cohesion and tensile strength in the absence of moisture or particle cementation [2]. Strength data also help to infer density, porosity and layering in the upper regolith [7]. Such data underpin both science about the regolith's physical state and every engineering activity that must dig, anchor or build on the surface. Because the strength values reported for the Moon depend on the instrument, the test method and the interpretation model, each value must be traced to the specific instrument and test.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or strength specification for a soil mechanical properties tester. The examples below describe specific instruments. Values left blank were not found in the sources consulted and are not estimated.

examples.name: Surveyor soil mechanics surface sampler (Surveyor 3 and Surveyor 7)
examples.type: Historical lunar instrument, flown on Surveyor 3 and Surveyor 7 landers

examples.qualification: Surveyor 7 record [1] gives temperature range and construction. Mass and dimensions not stated in sources consulted.

examples.type: Proposed concept evaluated in laboratory tests on lunar simulants; not flown

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions and proportions: the best-documented dimensions are those of the Apollo SRP bearing plate and cones, which are small compared with a lander [4]. No overall dimensions were found for the SRP or the Surveyor surface sampler in the sources consulted [5][6].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass and weight: no mass was found in the sources consulted for either the Apollo SRP or the Surveyor surface sampler [5][1]. Mass values should not be inferred from other instruments or from mission-level packages.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements: power source and consumption were not specified in the sources consulted. For the Surveyor sampler, motor current was recorded during tests [1].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The sampler and penetrometer operated in the lunar vacuum and thermal environment, which exposes equipment to large temperature swings. The Surveyor 7 record reports a sampler operating range of +180 degrees F to -167 degrees F [1]. The Apollo SRP was operated by astronauts on the surface, with its reference plane resting on the regolith while a cone or the bearing plate was pushed in [4]. A vacuum-chamber penetrometer study reported that off-gassing disturbed simulant strength results, although slowing the pump rate reduced the disturbance [8]. Strength results depend on density, layering and test location, so the site and depth of each test should be recorded alongside the data.
article.limitations: The class has no universal specification, and penetration and trenching data are indirect. Results depend on interpretation models and assumptions about soil friction [4]. Several reported values are available only as search summaries and are flagged in the uncertainties section below. Laboratory results on simulants may not reproduce lunar behaviour. In one laboratory study, none of the field instruments tested was judged adequate for a low-cohesion, frictional soil [3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Historical examples were delivered as part of uncrewed Surveyor landers (the surface sampler) and as a crew-operated experiment on Apollo 15 and Apollo 16 (the SRP) [1][4][5]. The sources consulted do not give interface, mass or power data that would allow compatibility with any particular lander to be assessed.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument or sampler onto the lander or into the surface payload on Earth, which for Surveyor meant mounting the sampler on the spacecraft [1].
Launch and transfer to the Moon.
Land and operate the instrument on the surface. For Surveyor, the sampler dug, pressed and trenched the surface while its motor current was recorded and cameras imaged the sampled material [1][6].
For Apollo 15 and 16, astronauts operated the SRP at test stations on the surface, with the reference plane resting on the regolith [4][7].
Record and return data, using the SRP's recording drum and Surveyor telemetry [4][6].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surveyor: the sampler was mounted on the lander and operated by command, with data limited by telemetry [1][6]. Apollo: the SRP was operated manually by astronauts during EVA [4][7]. A future instrument's deployment method would depend on its mission design.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Surveyor 3 and Surveyor 7 carried soil mechanics surface samplers [1][6]. Apollo 15 and 16 carried the Self-Recording Penetrometer [4][5]. A modified shear vane was evaluated in the laboratory as a concept [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not assessed. Compatibility with a specific lander would need verified mass, dimensions, mounting interface, deployment method, power and data interfaces, none of which were verified here.

article.historical_significance: The Surveyor soil mechanics surface sampler was the first surface soil scoop carried on a lunar mission, according to a search summary of the Smithsonian record [6]. The Apollo SRP produced penetration-resistance profiles at several Apollo 15 and 16 stations [4][5][7]. Apollo-era strength values were obtained largely by indirect methods such as trenching, penetration and vane shear [2]. Later mission and laboratory work built on these data, but the sources consulted do not establish a continuous lineage of flown soil tester designs.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: 'Soil mechanical properties tester' describes a class of instruments, not one design, and the examples are not interchangeable. Penetrometer results depend on an interpretation model. The SRP report notes that many combinations of cohesion and friction angle satisfy the same penetration equation, so unique values need additional measurements, such as two cone sizes in the same soil or resistance at two depths in a homogeneous deposit [4]. The SRP analysis assumes a soil-to-plate friction ratio of 0.5, taken from friction tests on a ground-basalt simulant rather than lunar soil [4], and its failure model was checked only in model tests on dense, fine, sandy soils [4]. Apollo-era strength values, including friction angles between 30 and 50 degrees and a lower-bound cohesion of 0.03 to 0.10 kN/m2 at the Apollo 14 trench site, come from a search summary of NASA soil mechanics material and were not verified in full text [7]. For Surveyor 3, force and motor-current data were reported as not obtained because of telemetry problems after landing, according to a search summary that was not checked against the primary record [6]. A vacuum-chamber penetrometer study reported that off-gassing affected simulant strength results and that slower pumping reduced the disturbance, but its PDF could not be read in this run [8]. The generic environmental and deployment discussion is an engineering summary, not a certified design specification.
